newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Doctors seek ways to reduce mothers' deaths.
newsitem.headline: Doctors seek ways to reduce mothers' deaths.

text.p: Medical experts ended a five-day meeting in Morocco on Friday focused on millions of deaths of women in childbirth and seeking ways to cut the toll.

Repeatedly citing African and Asian mothers as the main victims, the congress asked the 750 delegates to draw up ideas for sending specialists to one country to build an "experimental village" where the world could be shown the number of deaths could be reduced.

"No specific recommendations were issued because it is a purely scientific gathering...But all participants in their speeches urged the world community to mobilise for a solution to this tragedy," Badr Tazi, a Moroccan doctor and congress spokesman, told Reuters.
Dr Daniel Weinstein, president of the World Society on Labor and Delivery, said six million women had died in childbirth since 1990, and it was "an international challenge" to reduce this.

He said he would continue to seek to "raise the necessary funds" to send a medical team to a country suffering high maternal mortality "and prove to the world community that it is possible to put an end to this human tragedy".

During the congress, Malian gynaecology professor Dolo Amado told reporters that African women ran 15 to 30 times more risk of dying through childbirth complication than women in Asia, and 100 times more than women in Europe.
But with changed attitudes, more finance and greater general medical care for pregnant women, this could change.

Amado said that in Mali, where women's groups and the health department had cooperated in campaigning to cut deaths, maternal mortality in two years had fallen to 570 deaths per 100,000 live births from 700.

Tazi said congress workshops, like one on community medicine, had "shown how community health care in remote areas of Africa and Asia is so important and often very efficient in reducing the continuing maternal mortality tragedy".

Weinstein told the conference attended by doctors, midwives and other specialists from 76 countries: "This tragedy is worse than AIDS, even more than the Holocaust, because millions of women will continue to die every year if no urgent measures are taken by the world community."
